description: This working paper develops a two-structure framework for analyzing AI power in the emerging AI order. It distinguishes AI National Power, defined as the usable capacity of a national system to generate, mobilize, govern, and sustain AI-relevant resources, from AI Boundary Power, defined as an actor-level relational capacity to alter another actor's access to AI-relevant resources at a specified interface. The paper further separates boundary control from target-side boundary autonomy and from systemic influence as a later outcome. Through mechanism illustrations involving advanced-computing export controls and European Union AI regulation, it argues that national depth and boundary control are distinct but potentially complementary forms of AI power.
abstract: Artificial intelligence competition is often measured through models, compute, investment, and adoption, yet these indicators conflate resources, relational leverage, and system-level outcomes. This article develops a two-structure framework that distinguishes AI National Power (ANP) from AI Boundary Power (ABP). ANP is the usable capacity of a national system to generate, mobilize, govern, and sustain AI-relevant resources. ABP is an actor-level relational capacity to alter the conditions under which another actor can obtain, transfer, integrate, deploy, or continue using an AI-relevant resource at a specified interface. The framework further separates boundary control from target-side boundary autonomy and from systemic influence as a later outcome. Through conceptual synthesis, operationalization, and mechanism illustrations involving advanced-computing export controls and European Union AI regulation, the article identifies effective control, interface criticality, enforceability, substitutability, and organizational conversion as key conditioning mechanisms. It argues that national depth and boundary control are distinct but potentially complementary forms of AI power. Their interaction helps explain why technologically capable states may remain externally constrained, why narrower actors can exercise consequential leverage, and why durable influence depends on more than possession of advanced AI.

methodology.source_basis: Conceptual synthesis, operationalization, and mechanism-centered comparison using AI governance literature, technology-sovereignty research, network and structural power theory, regulatory power theory, export-control evidence, and European Union AI regulation.
methodology.case_context: Theoretical framework development with bounded mechanism illustrations involving U.S. advanced-computing export controls and European Union general-purpose AI regulation.
methodology.core_problem: The central analytical problem is how AI power should be conceptualized when national capability, control over consequential interfaces, target-side autonomy, and durable system-level effects do not coincide.
central_claims: AI power should not be reduced to model benchmarks, compute, investment, or adoption because these indicators conflate resources, relational leverage, and outcomes.
AI National Power is a state-level construct concerning usable national capacity to generate, mobilize, govern, and sustain AI-relevant resources.
AI Boundary Power is a controller-target-interface-time relation concerning effective control over another actor's access to AI-relevant resources or functions.
Boundary autonomy is a target-side capacity to reduce exposure to another actor's boundary control.
Systemic influence is a later outcome and should not be inferred directly from high ANP or high ABP.
National depth and boundary control are distinct but potentially complementary forms of AI power.
Durable influence depends on organizational conversion, effective control, interface criticality, target substitutability, enforceability, adaptation, and network structure.

analytical_lenses.name: AI National Power
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses usable national-system capacity to generate, sustain, mobilize, govern, and convert AI-relevant resources into specified effects.

analytical_lenses.name: AI Boundary Power
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses controller-target-interface-time relations in which an actor alters another actor's ability to obtain, transfer, integrate, deploy, or continue using AI-relevant resources.

analytical_lenses.name: Boundary Autonomy
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses target-side switching, multi-homing, bypass, substitution, redesign, localization, and internalization capacity.

analytical_lenses.name: Systemic Influence
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses persistent and sufficiently broad changes in feasible option sets, network connections, or governing rules in a pre-specified domain.

analytical_lenses.name: Organizational Conversion
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses how resource stocks become usable national capability through coordination, procurement, authority, implementation institutions, and resilience.

analytical_lenses.name: Interface Control
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses effective discretion, criticality, enforceability, and substitutability at AI-relevant boundaries.

analytical_lenses.name: Measurement Role Separation
analytical_lenses.description: Separates resource inputs, conversion mechanisms, constructs, target autonomy, and later outcomes to reduce circularity.

dimensions.name: AI National Power
dimensions.description: Usable capacity of a territorially and politically constituted national system to generate, sustain, mobilize, govern, and convert AI-relevant resources into economic, administrative, scientific, social, and strategic effects.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Resource bases include territorial-infrastructural capacity, human-epistemic capacity, and economic-industrial capacity; conversion depends on political-administrative mobilization.
dimensions.interpretation: Presence of assets is not equivalent to mobilizable national capability.

dimensions.name: AI Boundary Power
dimensions.description: Effective capacity of an actor to change the conditions under which another actor can obtain, transfer, integrate, deploy, or continue using an AI-relevant resource or function at a specified interface.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Observed through licensing, pricing, authentication, filtering/throttling, interoperability, certification, standards, procurement, market access, denial, or termination.
dimensions.interpretation: ABP is a controller-target-interface-time relation rather than a generic actor-level stock.

dimensions.name: Boundary Autonomy
dimensions.description: Capacity of a target to reduce exposure to another actor's boundary control through switching, multi-homing, bypass, substitution, redesign, localization, or internalization.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Greater pre-intervention substitutability should reduce subsequent access or deployment-capacity losses under comparable restrictions.
dimensions.interpretation: Boundary autonomy can reduce vulnerability without making the target a gatekeeper.

dimensions.name: Systemic Influence
dimensions.description: Persistent and sufficiently broad changes in other actors' feasible option sets, network connections, or governing rules within a pre-specified domain.
dimensions.observed_pattern: May appear as durable standards adoption, network rewiring, repeated architecture changes, supply-chain redesign, or compliance spillovers.
dimensions.interpretation: Systemic influence is not guaranteed by high ANP, high ABP, or one strong boundary intervention.

dimensions.name: Effective Control
dimensions.description: Actual discretion over relevant access conditions or terms.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Formal authority alone does not establish consequential ABP without discretion and implementation ability.
dimensions.interpretation: Control must be documented at the relevant interface.

dimensions.name: Interface Criticality
dimensions.description: Functional importance of the controlled interface for the target's intended task.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Restrictions matter more when the interface is difficult to avoid or replace for the target's use case.
dimensions.interpretation: A central interface may have low leverage if it is not critical to the target.

dimensions.name: Substitutability
dimensions.description: Availability, quality, cost, and timing of alternative routes, suppliers, standards, or internal capacity.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Higher switching costs and longer substitution times should increase restrictive boundary effects.
dimensions.interpretation: ABP rises as target substitutability decreases.

dimensions.name: Enforceability
dimensions.description: Ability to enforce changed access conditions at acceptable political, legal, technical, or commercial cost.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Weak enforcement can reduce the realized effect of formally strong boundary conditions.
dimensions.interpretation: Legal rules are insufficient without practical enforcement.

key_findings: AI competition is often measured through indicators that conflate resources, relational leverage, autonomy, and outcomes.
AI National Power and AI Boundary Power should be treated as distinct analytical structures.
ANP concerns usable national-system capacity, not simple possession of domestic AI assets.
ABP concerns relational control at a specified interface, not generic national or actor-level power.
Boundary autonomy belongs to the target side and should not be collapsed into boundary control.
Systemic influence is a later outcome requiring persistence and breadth.
National depth and boundary control can be complementary but are not jointly sufficient to guarantee systemic influence.
The European Union can exercise AI Boundary Power through market-access regulation even though ANP is reserved for states.
U.S. advanced-computing export controls illustrate compute-boundary control through jurisdiction, licensing, product coverage, and enforcement.
Product redesign and subsequent rule expansion illustrate that boundary power can migrate, persist, or dissipate depending on adjacent scarcity and target substitution.

Middle powers can build AI agency through selective capacity, boundary architecture, supplier diversification, interoperability, trusted partnerships, and fallback arrangements rather than full-stack autarky.
policy_recommendations: Separate national AI capacity, interface-level boundary control, target-side autonomy, and systemic influence in AI power assessment.
Do not treat model benchmarks, compute totals, investment, or adoption as a single AI power leaderboard without specifying mechanism and unit of analysis.
Measure ANP by sector and time horizon through resource bases, mobilizability, organizational conversion, and usable capability.
Measure ABP through boundary maps that identify controller, target, interface, direction, time window, discretion, criticality, substitutability, and enforceability.
Treat boundary autonomy as a core resilience variable for states, firms, and institutions exposed to externally controlled AI interfaces.
Code systemic influence only when durable and broad changes are demonstrated within a pre-specified domain.

For middle powers, prioritize diversified suppliers, interoperable architectures, trusted partnerships, public digital infrastructure, standards expertise, and fallback arrangements rather than attempting full-stack autarky in every layer.

For regulators, distinguish jurisdictional ABP from proven system-level spillover and measure whether compliance architectures, product designs, or market-entry rules persist beyond initial implementation.

propositions.title: Substitutability conditions restrictive boundary effects
propositions.statement: For comparably exposed targets facing restrictions of similar severity and functional scope, higher pre-intervention switching costs and longer substitution times should be associated with larger subsequent losses of deployment capacity.

propositions.title: Organizational conversion conditions national capacity
propositions.statement: Holding technical resource stocks approximately constant, states with stronger lawful coordination, procurement, implementation, and mobilization capacity should convert a larger share of those resources into usable sectoral AI capability.

propositions.title: National depth and state boundary power are complementary but not jointly sufficient
propositions.statement: Among states compared over the same sector, target set, and time window, the marginal association between ANP and the breadth and durability of external influence should increase as effective state ABP rises, while high ANP and high ABP at an initial time do not guarantee systemic influence.

propositions.title: Boundary autonomy reduces vulnerability
propositions.statement: Among targets facing restrictions of similar severity, greater pre-intervention switching, bypass, substitution, or internalization capacity should be associated with smaller subsequent losses of access or deployment capacity.

propositions.title: Boundary erosion can produce migration or dissipation of power
propositions.statement: When substitution reduces control at one AI layer, leverage should move to an adjacent interface only if that interface remains scarce and consequential; otherwise, overall boundary power should decline rather than automatically migrate.
